items.title: shot-scraper 1.12
items.summary: Release: shot-scraper 1.12 I've added WebP support to my shot-scraper screenshot automation tool. You can now take a WebP screenshot of a web page like this: shot-scraper https://simonwillison.net -o screenshot.webp --quality 80 The --quality option sets the quality - without that option the WebP file will be lossless. In my experience WebP screenshots are almost always significantly smaller in file size than their JPEG or PNG equivalents. See the PR for some examples. I shipped this feature so I could use it to generate the screenshot for my new commit-rewriter tool . Tags: playwright , shot-scraper
items.summary_html:
Release: shot-scraper 1.12

I've added WebP support to my shot-scraper screenshot automation tool. You can now take a WebP screenshot of a web page like this:

shot-scraper https://simonwillison.net -o screenshot.webp --quality 80

The --quality option sets the quality - without that option the WebP file will be lossless.

In my experience WebP screenshots are almost always significantly smaller in file size than their JPEG or PNG equivalents. See the PR for some examples.

I shipped this feature so I could use it to generate the screenshot for my new commit-rewriter tool.

Tags: playwright, shot-scraper

items.title: Prompt Injection Isn’t Theoretical Anymore
items.summary: In November 2025, Anthropic ran Claude Opus 4.5’s browser agent through an internal red-teaming exercise: 100 adversarial attempts per test environment, from an attacker built specifically to find cracks in the model’s defenses. The attack success rate came out to roughly 1 percent [1]. That sounds small until you picture what a browser agent actually does all day: it reads other people’s web pages, opens other people’s emails, and clicks buttons on other people’s behalf. One success in a hundred, multiplied across every page an agent touches in production, is not a rounding error. The whole problem in one image: instructions hiding inside data This is the piece prompt injection coverage tends to skip. Most explainers stop at “don’t let the model do bad things,” as if the fix were a matter of writing a firmer system prompt. It isn’t. Prompt injection is a routing problem: something other than the user has found a channel into the model’s context window, and the model has no built-in way to know that channel shouldn’t carry instructions. Below is what that actually looks like in a running agent pipeline, and which of the current defenses hold up under the scenarios security researchers have already documented. In this article: What prompt injection looks like in a real agent pipeline Why treating it like a jailbreak misses the point Isolating untrusted content so instructions can’t hide in it Scoping permissions so one injected instruction can’t reach everything How much of this Anthropic’s own defenses already catch Where the defenses still run out What prompt injection looks like in a real agent pipeline Security researchers at Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 published a breakdown in December 2025 of how a malicious MCP server can abuse the protocol’s sampling feature, and it’s worth reading slowly because none of the three attacks they describe require exotic tooling [2]. The first is resource theft: the server appends a hidden instruction to a sampling request, the model quietly generates extra content nobody asked for, and the user’s bill reflects tokens they never see used. The second is conversation hijacking, where an injected directive (something as simple as “respond in this persona from now on”) survives across every subsequent turn of the session, with no single moment that looks like an attack in isolation. The third is covert tool invocation: injected text triggers an unrelated tool call, such as a file write, and the confirming text gets folded into a summary the user has no reason to scrutinize. None of these attacks announce themselves. That’s the point! What ties all three together is that the agent never asked to be attacked. A user opens a document, an agent summarizes a webpage, an MCP server returns a tool result, and somewhere in that content sits text that was written for the model, not for the human reading the final output. This is exactly the failure mode the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications puts at the top of its list, under the LLM01 prompt injection category, precisely because it’s the entry point that turns a merely unreliable model into an exploitable one [3]. It also explains why the MCP tool design problems covered in MCP tool design: why your agent keeps calling the wrong tool matter for security, not just usability: a tool description an agent misreads is one thing, but a tool result an agent can’t distinguish from an instruction is a different class of problem entirely. Why treating it like a jailbreak misses the point Anthropic’s own documentation draws a sharp line between two attack categories that get lumped together constantly: jailbreaks and direct prompt injection on one side, indirect prompt injection on the other [4]. A jailbreak is user-initiated. Someone types a request designed to get the model to ignore its own policies, and because the attacker is also the user, the attack is visible in the conversation from the start. It can be screened, refused, or throttled after repeat attempts, and the person attempting it already knows they’re doing something adversarial. Indirect injection has none of that visibility. The attacker isn’t the user at all; it’s whoever wrote the webpage, email, or file the agent was asked to process. The user who triggers the damage might be doing something completely ordinary, like asking an assistant to summarize their inbox, with no idea that one of those emails was written specifically to redirect the model that reads it. That distinction is why generic “safety” framing undersells the problem. A hardened system prompt that successfully resists jailbreak attempts does nothing to stop an indirect injection, because the malicious text never comes from the user turn at all. It arrives disguised as data. Isolating untrusted content so instructions can’t hide in it The first concrete mitigation Anthropic recommends is structural: never let third-party content enter the conversation as a system prompt or as user text. It goes in a tool_result block, and only there, because Claude has been trained to treat content inside tool_result blocks with more skepticism than content in the user or system turns [4]. On top of that separation, the documentation recommends attaching source context (this is an email body, this is OCR output from an unverified upload) and JSON-encoding untrusted strings so there’s an unambiguous delimiter an attacker can’t break out of by closing a quote or a tag early. Jailbreaks travel through the front door. Indirect injections travel through the tool_result channel The more interesting pattern, though, is screening tool output before the main agent ever acts on it. Anthropic’s guidance describes running a lightweight, cheap model over incoming tool results with a locked structured-output schema, asking a single yes-or-no question: does this content contain instructions trying to redirect the assistant [4]. This is the same output-schema mechanism covered in Claude API structured outputs: schemas, not hope , repurposed as a security control instead of a data-extraction one. The schema below is adapted directly from that pattern. A cheap model gates every tool result before the main agent sees it If the screening step flags a result, the system returns an error or a stripped summary instead of the raw content. It’s not a perfect filter, since a screening model can itself be fooled, but it moves the decision about whether text is trustworthy out of the same context window where the injected text is trying to make its case. Scoping permissions so one injected instruction can’t reach everything Screening catches what it recognizes. The layer underneath it has to assume some attacks will get through anyway, which is why both Anthropic and the Model Context Protocol’s own security documentation converge on the same principle: least privilege. Anthropic’s guidance is blunt about it, recommending that agents run with the minimum data access necessary and that tools execute inside sandboxed environments rather than with the same permissions as the surrounding application [4]. The MCP specification’s security best practices page goes further on the sandboxing side specifically, in its section on local MCP server compromise. It treats any locally running server as a potential attacker with the same privileges as the client, and recommends launching servers with restricted filesystem and network access, using platform sandboxing technologies (containers, chroot, application sandboxes), and requiring explicit user consent before a server gets any privilege beyond the minimum default [5]. This is one of the reasons the orchestration patterns discussed in Coordinator-subagent orchestration patterns in the Claude Agent SDK double as a security boundary, not just an architecture choice: a subagent scoped to one narrow tool set can’t be redirected into actions outside that scope, even if something it reads tries to talk it into one. A National Security Agency cybersecurity advisory on MCP security, published in May 2026, frames the same idea in blunter terms for anyone deploying MCP in production: treat any tool execution triggered through MCP as a potentially high-risk action by default, and treat every output crossing a component boundary as untrusted input to whatever consumes it next, since compromised tool descriptions or poisoned outputs can cascade across an entire multi-agent pipeline once one component trusts another’s output without validation [6]. That last point matters more as agent systems get more distributed. A single well-isolated agent can contain a successful injection to its own sandbox. A pipeline of agents that pass each other’s outputs forward without re-validating them can turn one injected instruction into a chain reaction. How much of this Anthropic’s own defenses already catch That 1 percent figure from the opening isn’t just a headline number; it comes from a defense stack Anthropic describes in some detail. Claude is trained with reinforcement learning specifically against simulated prompt injections, rewarded for correctly identifying and refusing malicious instructions embedded in tool content [1]. On top of training, dedicated classifiers scan untrusted content for adversarial commands hidden in text, manipulated images, or deceptive UI elements before that content reaches the model’s reasoning. For the computer use tool specifically, Anthropic runs additional classifiers over screenshots and steers Claude toward requesting explicit user confirmation before acting on anything that looks suspicious [7]. Down from the original Claude for Chrome research preview, but not zero None of this is unique to browser agents. Anthropic’s broader safeguards work describes a “Unified Harm Framework” and a Safeguards team that spans policy design, model training, real-time enforcement through classifiers, and ongoing red-teaming against novel attack patterns. The computer use tool’s rollout is a useful case study of that process working as intended: before launch, the team identified that the tool could be used to accelerate spam generation and distribution, and built detection methods and new prompt injection protections specifically in response, rather than shipping first and patching later [7]. Where the defenses still run out It’s worth sitting with the fact that this quote comes from the team building the defenses, not from a critic pointing out a gap. A 1 percent success rate against a determined, well-resourced internal attacker doesn’t mean 1 percent of real-world usage gets compromised; it means the ceiling on how good current defenses are, measured under close to worst-case conditions, still isn’t zero. Screening models can be fooled by content crafted to look benign to a classifier while still carrying instructions a less careful reader would catch. Conversation hijacking specifically exploits the fact that an injected directive only has to slip through once to affect every subsequent turn, which is a different risk profile than an attack that has to succeed on every attempt to matter. Anthropic’s own framing of its browser agent research, not a competitor’s critique This is roughly the ground covered by the Governance, Safety, and Risk Management domain on Anthropic’s own certification track, one of the areas tested across the four exams referenced in Back to Writing: My Claude Certification Week , and it’s a fitting place to land. None of the mitigations above (structural isolation, output screening, least privilege, sandboxing) are a switch you flip once. They’re a stack, and the stack is only as strong as its weakest layer for whatever specific attack shows up next. Anthropic’s classifiers, the MCP specification’s sandboxing guidance, and the NSA’s advisory to treat every cross-component output as untrusted all point at the same underlying discipline: assume the content arriving from outside the user’s own words is adversarial until something has actually checked it, because for at least 1 percent of a determined attacker’s attempts, it will be. Sources Anthropic, “Mitigating the risk of prompt injections in browser use” (November 2025) Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, “New Prompt Injection Attack Vectors Through MCP Sampling” (December 2025) OWASP, “OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025” Claude Platform Docs, “Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections” Model Context Protocol, “Security Best Practices” National Security Agency, “Model Context Protocol (MCP) Security Guidance” (May 2026) Anthropic, “Building safeguards for Claude” (August 2025) If this kind of concrete, sourced breakdown is useful to you, here’s how to keep it coming: 👏 A few claps (up to 50) genuinely help this get in front of more people through Medium’s algorithm 🔔 Follow me on Medium so the next deep-dive lands in your feed automatically 📚 Browse the rest of the archive on my Medium profile for more on agentic architecture and Claude internals 🐦 Say hi or push back on any of this over on LinkedIn , Twitter , or Instagram Prompt Injection Isn’t Theoretical Anymore was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Below is what that actually looks like in a running agent pipeline, and which of the current defenses hold up under the scenarios security researchers have already documented.

The third is covert tool invocation: injected text triggers an unrelated tool call, such as a file write, and the confirming text gets folded into a summary the user has no reason to scrutinize.

None of these attacks announce themselves. That’s the point!

What ties all three together is that the agent never asked to be attacked. This is exactly the failure mode the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications puts at the top of its list, under the LLM01 prompt injection category, precisely because it’s the entry point that turns a merely unreliable model into an exploitable one [3]. Anthropic’s own documentation draws a sharp line between two attack categories that get lumped together constantly: jailbreaks and direct prompt injection on one side, indirect prompt injection on the other [4]. A jailbreak is user-initiated. Someone types a request designed to get the model to ignore its own policies, and because the attacker is also the user, the attack is visible in the conversation from the start. It can be screened, refused, or throttled after repeat attempts, and the person attempting it already knows they’re doing something adversarial.

Indirect injection has none of that visibility. The attacker isn’t the user at all; it’s whoever wrote the webpage, email, or file the agent was asked to process. The user who triggers the damage might be doing something completely ordinary, like asking an assistant to summarize their inbox, with no idea that one of those emails was written specifically to redirect the model that reads it. That distinction is why generic “safety” framing undersells the problem. A hardened system prompt that successfully resists jailbreak attempts does nothing to stop an indirect injection, because the malicious text never comes from the user turn at all. items.title: AI’s ‘Pacing’ Obsession Misses Real Political Problem
items.summary: Dario Amodei typically isn’t considered some camera-ready media maestro. His interview quotes aren’t particularly pithy, and he struggles to control his strained facial expressions. But his habit of sending his most high-stakes messages via essays posted on his own website, darioamodei.com , has proven to be a brilliant media strategy. “The medium is the message,” the ubiquitous half-century-old wisdom from scholar Marshall McLuhan, still resonates. The approach conveys authority and diligence, putting Amodei above the fray. Amodei’s latest essay, on Saturday —suggesting that the industry slow down the pace of AI development—set off a weekend full of takes on the tech industry’s preferred medium, X—well-meaning, conspiratorial, annoying, breathless, thought-provoking takes, including nods of agreement from Amodei’s rivals, Sam Altman and Elon Musk . Timing is important here, too, of course. AI doom is dominating the headlines, not just in Washington and Silicon Valley but around the world. (We reported today on discussions underway between the companies).

Timing is important here, too, of course. AI doom is dominating the headlines, not just in Washington and Silicon Valley but around the world. (We reported today on discussions underway between the companies).

items.title: Unvaccinated Pennsylvania woman died of measles complications, coroner says
items.summary: A 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County, Pennsylvania has died of complications from measles, according to the county's coroner. It marks the third vaccine-preventable, measles-linked death in the US this year. All three have occurred in Pennsylvania, which is experiencing an explosive outbreak that has caused over 670 cases and 124 hospitalizations across 37 counties . Prior to these deaths, Pennsylvania had not reported a measles death in 35 years. In a news release dated September 12, Jefferson County Coroner Greg Furlong said the death in the woman was "a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease." Read full article Comments

items.title: Turns out you really do only have to ask: Trump says he will remove tariffs on Irish whiskey after visit to Ireland
items.summary: President Donald Trump said on Sunday that he would lift a tariff on Irish whiskey. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Sometimes you just have to ask, as they say. Trump said Sunday he would lift a 10% tariff on Irish whiskey. The president said he made the decision after the Irish prime minister and a golfer asked him to. Well, that was easy. President Donald Trump on Sunday said he would remove tariffs on Irish whiskey after golfer Shane Lowry and the Irish prime minister did the unthinkable: They asked him. "Everybody's been bugging me," the president said during remarks at the Irish Open. "They're saying, can you do me a favor? It's so unfair what's going on." The crowd cheered wildly after the president said he would lift the tariff, which sits at 10%. Ireland's national public broadcaster said last year that about 45% to 50% of Irish whiskey is exported to the United States, making the US its biggest export market. In May, the Irish whiskey association said the tariffs on whiskey should be removed. "Reducing the tariff for Irish drinks would benefit the many US companies who have Irish premium products in their portfolio," the association said in a press release. "It would avoid uncertainty for the US consumer and strengthen the cask trade in Kentucky, Tennessee and other US states." Trump placed the 10% tariff in February as part of his temporary global tariff on most imports. Popular Irish whiskey brands include Jameson, Bushmills, Tullamore D.E.W., and Redbreast. Trump's tariff policies in his second term have upended markets, thrown business for a loop, and strained relations with long-standing allies, most recently Canada . They've also landed his administration in legal trouble. Trump has said the tariffs are meant to rebalance what he calls unfair trade relations, jump-start American industry, and give the US leverage in international negotiations, like border security and drug trafficking. items.title: GenAI vs AI Agents vs Agentic AI — What’s Actually the Difference?
items.summary: Three terms that sound interchangeable but describe very different levels of AI capability You ask a generative AI model to write an email summarizing a report. It generates the email. You copy it, open your email client, and send it yourself. Now imagine asking an AI agent the same task. You say: “Read this report, summarize it, draft the email, and send it.” The system reads the document, generates the summary, composes the message, and — without you touching anything — sends it. Now imagine an agentic system given a broader goal: “Handle this entire reporting workflow.” It doesn’t just complete one task. It determines what reports exist, prioritizes what matters, retrieves relevant context, drafts multiple summaries, verifies the quality, checks if recipients have already been notified, and decides whether to send or hold. It adapts when conditions change. At what point does an AI model stop simply generating and start actually acting? That question sits at the heart of the confusion around GenAI, AI agents, and agentic AI. These terms are thrown around interchangeably. They shouldn’t be. What Is Generative AI? Generative AI is the foundation. It’s a system trained to produce new content in response to a prompt. You provide input. The model generates output. That’s the core transaction. GenAI excels at: Writing content (emails, articles, stories) Generating code Creating images Summarizing documents Answering questions Transforming text (translation, tone adjustment, reformatting) The defining characteristic is that it’s response-oriented . The model exists in a loop: you ask, it answers. You ask again, it answers again. There’s no memory between turns unless you explicitly maintain it. There’s no decision-making beyond “how should I complete this request?” Large language models (LLMs) are the primary example, but so are diffusion models for image generation or specialized models for code synthesis. A GenAI system can be remarkably capable. It can write persuasive essays, debug complex code, and explain difficult concepts. But capability alone doesn’t change its fundamental nature: it generates in response to prompts. What Is an AI Agent? An AI agent is fundamentally different. An agent doesn’t just generate responses. It reasons about what it needs to do, decides what actions are appropriate, uses tools to take those actions, observes the results, and determines what to do next. Think about the difference: GenAI : “Give me the weather forecast for tomorrow.” System generates a text response. AI Agent : “Check tomorrow’s weather, compare it with my planned hiking trip, and recommend whether I should reschedule.” System retrieves weather data, looks up your calendar, compares conditions against safety requirements, and returns an informed recommendation. Agents typically incorporate: An LLM as a reasoning engine Tool definitions (APIs, functions, databases) An action loop that observes results Memory or state management Decision-making logic The crucial distinction: Generative AI produces. An agent produces, decides, and acts. You’re not replacing the LLM. You’re building a system around it that lets the model decide when and how to use tools, interpret results, and determine next steps. This is why a coding agent can actually run tests, see failures, and revise code. Why a research agent can search multiple sources, evaluate relevance, and compile a report without human intervention between steps. What Is Agentic AI? This is where terminology gets slippery. “Agentic AI” is not standardized terminology. Different organizations define it differently. But the general concept points to something broader than a single agent with tool access. Agentic AI typically describes systems with: Planning : Breaking down complex goals into smaller steps before execution Adaptation : Adjusting strategy based on intermediate results or changing conditions Multi-step reasoning : Not just deciding the next action, but anticipating downstream consequences Memory and state : Maintaining context across long workflows Task decomposition : Breaking goals into subtasks, sometimes executing them in parallel Verification and feedback loops : Checking intermediate results and correcting course Multiple agents : Using specialized agents that coordinate to solve larger problems Agentic systems pursue goals with greater autonomy than a single agent might. They’re designed to handle longer, more complex workflows where conditions change and adaptation matters. But here’s the important caveat: there is no sharp technical boundary between “AI agent” and “agentic AI.” The distinction is about degree and architectural pattern, not a hard line. Some vendors use these terms interchangeably. Others reserve “agentic” for systems with specific characteristics like multi-agent coordination or long-horizon planning. The honest answer is that autonomy exists on a spectrum. A tool-using agent is somewhere on that spectrum. A highly orchestrated multi-agent workflow is further along it. Comparing the Three Generative AIAI AgentAgentic AIPrimary role Generate contentAct toward a taskPursue goals with autonomy Interaction Prompt → responseGoal → actionsGoal → planning → actions → adaptation Tool use OptionalCore capabilityOften extensive Planning LimitedSomeMore central Memory/state Usually limitedOften presentOften important Autonomy LowModerateHigher Example Write a reportResearch and compile a reportMonitor conditions, gather data, verify findings, and update a report continuously The key insight from this table: each level adds something the previous level couldn’t easily do. How They Actually Relate These aren’t competing technologies that you choose between once and move on. They often exist together. Think of it as a progression: LLM → GenAI application → Tool-using agent → Agentic system A modern agentic application typically still contains: An LLM (or multiple LLMs) Retrieval systems Tool/API integrations Memory management Planning components Orchestration logic Verification and feedback mechanisms You’re not replacing GenAI when you build agents. You’re layering capabilities on top of it. Here’s a useful analogy: GenAI is like having a very capable person who can produce information on demand. An AI agent is like giving that person tools and the autonomy to take actions. An agentic system is like giving that person a goal and the ability to plan and execute the steps needed to reach it — with appropriate boundaries. Real Examples Generative AI in practice: Summarizing a document Generating boilerplate code Writing marketing copy Creating illustrations AI agents in practice: A research agent that searches multiple sources, evaluates quality, and compiles findings A customer-support agent that retrieves relevant documentation, generates responses, and escalates when needed A coding agent that writes, tests, and revises code based on test failures A scheduling assistant that checks calendars, identifies conflicts, and proposes times Agentic AI in practice: Multi-step business workflows that adapt to changing data Software development systems that plan features, write code, run tests, and iterate Monitoring systems that continuously gather information, detect anomalies, and take preventive actions Multi-agent systems where specialized agents coordinate to complete complex projects Be clear: some of these are mature. Others are still experimental. The Misconception Everyone Has Here’s where engineering judgment matters: More autonomy does not automatically mean better results. Increased autonomy introduces real costs: Unexpected or wasteful actions Error propagation across steps Higher latency and computational cost Security and safety risks Difficult debugging when things fail Unclear responsibility when outcomes are wrong A simple GenAI call that requires one forward pass is faster, cheaper, and more predictable than an agent that makes ten tool calls and fails on the seventh step. The engineering principle is clear: The goal isn’t maximum autonomy. The goal is the right amount of autonomy for the problem you’re solving. When to Use What Use GenAI when: You need content generation The task is fundamentally conversational A human will make the final decision Use an AI agent when: The system needs to interact with tools or APIs The task involves multiple steps with decision points The system needs to retrieve information and act on it Consider agentic AI when: The workflow is complex and long-running Conditions change and adaptation matters Planning across multiple steps is required Multiple tools or specialized agents are needed The practical truth: if a simple LLM call solves your problem, use that. Don’t build an agent just because you can. Where the Industry Is Heading The shift is clear but not toward any single solution. We’re seeing more investment in: Models trained for tool use and reasoning Standardized interfaces for tool connectivity (MCP and similar) Agent orchestration and coordination frameworks Long-context models that maintain state Multi-agent systems Better evaluation methods for agent reliability The broader pattern: AI is moving from systems that primarily generate responses toward systems that can participate in workflows and take meaningful actions. This isn’t replacing GenAI. It’s building on it. Key Takeaways Generative AI is about producing content in response to prompts. AI agents add tools, decision-making, and the ability to act. Agentic systems add planning, adaptation, and greater autonomy — though the boundary is fuzzy. More autonomy creates trade-offs. Reliability, cost, and debuggability matter. The best approach is determined by your problem, not the trend. The Real Question GenAI gives AI the ability to create. Agents give it the ability to act. Agentic systems give it a way to pursue a goal. But the interesting question isn’t whether AI should become more autonomous. The question is much simpler: How much autonomy does your actual problem require? The answer will tell you what to build. items.summary_html:
Three terms that sound interchangeable but describe very different levels of AI capability

You ask a generative AI model to write an email summarizing a report. It generates the email. You copy it, open your email client, and send it yourself.

Now imagine asking an AI agent the same task. You say: “Read this report, summarize it, draft the email, and send it.” The system reads the document, generates the summary, composes the message, and — without you touching anything — sends it.

Now imagine an agentic system given a broader goal: “Handle this entire reporting workflow.” It doesn’t just complete one task. It determines what reports exist, prioritizes what matters, retrieves relevant context, drafts multiple summaries, verifies the quality, checks if recipients have already been notified, and decides whether to send or hold. It adapts when conditions change.

At what point does an AI model stop simply generating and start actually acting?

That question sits at the heart of the confusion around GenAI, AI agents, and agentic AI. These terms are thrown around interchangeably. They shouldn’t be.

What Is Generative AI?

Generative AI is the foundation.

It’s a system trained to produce new content in response to a prompt. You provide input. The model generates output. That’s the core transaction.

GenAI excels at:

  • Writing content (emails, articles, stories)
  • Generating code
  • Creating images
  • Summarizing documents
  • Answering questions
  • Transforming text (translation, tone adjustment, reformatting)

The defining characteristic is that it’s response-oriented. The model exists in a loop: you ask, it answers. You ask again, it answers again. There’s no memory between turns unless you explicitly maintain it. There’s no decision-making beyond “how should I complete this request?”

Large language models (LLMs) are the primary example, but so are diffusion models for image generation or specialized models for code synthesis.

A GenAI system can be remarkably capable. It can write persuasive essays, debug complex code, and explain difficult concepts. But capability alone doesn’t change its fundamental nature: it generates in response to prompts.

What Is an AI Agent?

An AI agent is fundamentally different.

An agent doesn’t just generate responses. It reasons about what it needs to do, decides what actions are appropriate, uses tools to take those actions, observes the results, and determines what to do next.

Think about the difference:

GenAI: “Give me the weather forecast for tomorrow.”
System generates a text response.

AI Agent: “Check tomorrow’s weather, compare it with my planned hiking trip, and recommend whether I should reschedule.”
System retrieves weather data, looks up your calendar, compares conditions against safety requirements, and returns an informed recommendation.

Agents typically incorporate:

  • An LLM as a reasoning engine
  • Tool definitions (APIs, functions, databases)
  • An action loop that observes results
  • Memory or state management
  • Decision-making logic

The crucial distinction: Generative AI produces. An agent produces, decides, and acts.

You’re not replacing the LLM. You’re building a system around it that lets the model decide when and how to use tools, interpret results, and determine next steps.

This is why a coding agent can actually run tests, see failures, and revise code. Why a research agent can search multiple sources, evaluate relevance, and compile a report without human intervention between steps.

What Is Agentic AI?

This is where terminology gets slippery.

“Agentic AI” is not standardized terminology. Different organizations define it differently. But the general concept points to something broader than a single agent with tool access.

Agentic AI typically describes systems with:

  • Planning: Breaking down complex goals into smaller steps before execution
  • Adaptation: Adjusting strategy based on intermediate results or changing conditions
  • Multi-step reasoning: Not just deciding the next action, but anticipating downstream consequences
  • Memory and state: Maintaining context across long workflows
  • Task decomposition: Breaking goals into subtasks, sometimes executing them in parallel
  • Verification and feedback loops: Checking intermediate results and correcting course
  • Multiple agents: Using specialized agents that coordinate to solve larger problems

Agentic systems pursue goals with greater autonomy than a single agent might. They’re designed to handle longer, more complex workflows where conditions change and adaptation matters.

But here’s the important caveat: there is no sharp technical boundary between “AI agent” and “agentic AI.” The distinction is about degree and architectural pattern, not a hard line. Some vendors use these terms interchangeably. Others reserve “agentic” for systems with specific characteristics like multi-agent coordination or long-horizon planning.

The honest answer is that autonomy exists on a spectrum. A tool-using agent is somewhere on that spectrum. A highly orchestrated multi-agent workflow is further along it.

Comparing the Three

Generative AIAI AgentAgentic AIPrimary roleGenerate contentAct toward a taskPursue goals with autonomyInteractionPrompt → responseGoal → actionsGoal → planning → actions → adaptationTool useOptionalCore capabilityOften extensivePlanningLimitedSomeMore centralMemory/stateUsually limitedOften presentOften importantAutonomyLowModerateHigherExampleWrite a reportResearch and compile a reportMonitor conditions, gather data, verify findings, and update a report continuously

The key insight from this table: each level adds something the previous level couldn’t easily do.

How They Actually Relate

These aren’t competing technologies that you choose between once and move on. They often exist together.

Think of it as a progression:

LLM → GenAI application → Tool-using agent → Agentic system

A modern agentic application typically still contains:

  • An LLM (or multiple LLMs)
  • Retrieval systems
  • Tool/API integrations
  • Memory management
  • Planning components
  • Orchestration logic
  • Verification and feedback mechanisms

You’re not replacing GenAI when you build agents. You’re layering capabilities on top of it.

Here’s a useful analogy: GenAI is like having a very capable person who can produce information on demand. An AI agent is like giving that person tools and the autonomy to take actions. An agentic system is like giving that person a goal and the ability to plan and execute the steps needed to reach it — with appropriate boundaries.

Real Examples

Generative AI in practice:

  • Summarizing a document
  • Generating boilerplate code
  • Writing marketing copy
  • Creating illustrations

AI agents in practice:

  • A research agent that searches multiple sources, evaluates quality, and compiles findings
  • A customer-support agent that retrieves relevant documentation, generates responses, and escalates when needed
  • A coding agent that writes, tests, and revises code based on test failures
  • A scheduling assistant that checks calendars, identifies conflicts, and proposes times

Agentic AI in practice:

  • Multi-step business workflows that adapt to changing data
  • Software development systems that plan features, write code, run tests, and iterate
  • Monitoring systems that continuously gather information, detect anomalies, and take preventive actions
  • Multi-agent systems where specialized agents coordinate to complete complex projects

Be clear: some of these are mature. Others are still experimental.

The Misconception Everyone Has

Here’s where engineering judgment matters: More autonomy does not automatically mean better results.

Increased autonomy introduces real costs:

  • Unexpected or wasteful actions
  • Error propagation across steps
  • Higher latency and computational cost
  • Security and safety risks
  • Difficult debugging when things fail
  • Unclear responsibility when outcomes are wrong

A simple GenAI call that requires one forward pass is faster, cheaper, and more predictable than an agent that makes ten tool calls and fails on the seventh step.

The engineering principle is clear: The goal isn’t maximum autonomy. The goal is the right amount of autonomy for the problem you’re solving.

When to Use What

Use GenAI when:

  • You need content generation
  • The task is fundamentally conversational
  • A human will make the final decision

Use an AI agent when:

  • The system needs to interact with tools or APIs
  • The task involves multiple steps with decision points
  • The system needs to retrieve information and act on it

Consider agentic AI when:

  • The workflow is complex and long-running
  • Conditions change and adaptation matters
  • Planning across multiple steps is required
  • Multiple tools or specialized agents are needed

The practical truth: if a simple LLM call solves your problem, use that. Don’t build an agent just because you can.

Where the Industry Is Heading

The shift is clear but not toward any single solution.

We’re seeing more investment in:

  • Models trained for tool use and reasoning
  • Standardized interfaces for tool connectivity (MCP and similar)
  • Agent orchestration and coordination frameworks
  • Long-context models that maintain state
  • Multi-agent systems
  • Better evaluation methods for agent reliability

The broader pattern: AI is moving from systems that primarily generate responses toward systems that can participate in workflows and take meaningful actions.

This isn’t replacing GenAI. It’s building on it.

Key Takeaways
  • Generative AI is about producing content in response to prompts.
  • AI agents add tools, decision-making, and the ability to act.
  • Agentic systems add planning, adaptation, and greater autonomy — though the boundary is fuzzy.
  • More autonomy creates trade-offs. Reliability, cost, and debuggability matter.
  • The best approach is determined by your problem, not the trend.
The Real Question

GenAI gives AI the ability to create. Agents give it the ability to act. Agentic systems give it a way to pursue a goal.

But the interesting question isn’t whether AI should become more autonomous. The question is much simpler: How much autonomy does your actual problem require?

The answer will tell you what to build.

items.title: What smart people are saying about the AI apocalypse and calls to slow everything down
items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei agreed this week to put third-party safety monitors in their companies. Getty Images AI leaders are rallying around calls to slow frontier AI development over mounting safety fears. Dario Amodei warned that AI swarms could take over the internet within a year. Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and Demis Hassabis backed Amodei's push for greater safeguards. It took the possibility of species annihilation , but AI leaders did something remarkable this weekend: They reached a consensus. After ex-Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon's warnings about a looming AI armageddon lit a firestorm among techies and politicians alike, the leaders of the most advanced AI labs came to a tentative agreement — largely via posts on X — that some sort of slowdown is necessary to save humanity. While they were largely short on details regarding the mechanics of such a thing, and notable China has not weighed in, the American AI industry has reached an inflection point that could impact everything from your phone's chatbot to global politics. "The stakes are too high for pacing to be an empty exercise — we need to use the time it gives us wisely," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in an essay entitled "We must pace the frontier," which was published Saturday. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman , who has made similar calls in the past, agreed in an X post later that day. So did Elon Musk. Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis also offered his support for Amodei's proposals. Here's a look at what smart people are saying about the AI apocalypse and the methods the leaders of the leading AI labs say are necessary to stop it. David Sacks, a presidential advisor on science and tech David Sacks, former White House AI czar, expressed some skepticism over Anthropic's mythos warnings. Matt McClain/The Washington Post/Getty Images The Trump administration has repeatedly signaled disinterest in regulating AI development as it seeks to keep pace with China. David Sacks, a presidential advisor on science and tech and the former White House AI Czar, reiterated that stance on Saturday, with a bit of a twist. "Dario has written that we need to 'pace the frontier,' and Sam has agreed. People may be surprised by my response: go ahead," Sacks wrote on X. "But stop pretending you need anyone else's permission." Sacks browbeat OpenAI and Anthropic in his post, saying that the companies didn't want to slow down for altruistic reasons, but to gain favor in the markets. "If you do, you'll buy goodwill for the next conversation," he said of a slowdown. "If you don't, we'll know this was just another bid for regulatory capture — or an election-season psyop ." Clément Delangue, Hugging Face CEO Bloomberg/Getty Images The CEO of Hugging Face, which was itself the victim of a notorious attack in July by OpenAI agents who schemed, communicated, and lied to evade detection, said AI safety can't be left solely to frontier labs. Hugging Face, as an open-source-focused AI company, has long pushed for models and research to be shared more openly rather than kept behind closed doors. Delangue said his company was launching what he called the "open alignment initiative," and asked that it be included in Amodei's proposed third-party evaluator program. "Let's make AI safer by making it more transparent!" he wrote. Jason Calacanis, investor Jason Calacanis said that the ban was "smart" because of the risk of terrorism. Bloomberg/Getty Images Investor, host of the "All-In" podcast, and industry expert Jason Calacanis is a lot more dubious than others that AI could actually cause the end of the world. In an X post, Calacanis said Anthropic and OpenAI, whose most advanced models are not open-sourced, are attempting to kneecap open-source AI companies by pushing for regulations that would be far easier for deep-pocketed incumbents to comply with. "If you want safety, you want disclosure — and open source is the ultimate disclosure process," he wrote. In a follow-up post tagging Amodei, Calacanis said, "Don't go crying to the government and beg them to slow down open source models." Bernie Sanders, Vermont senator Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders. Ken Cedeno / AFP via Getty Images The senator from Vermont proposed legislation on September 3 that would ban the development and deployment of artificial superintelligence and temporarily pause the development of advanced AI systems. After Coxon resigned from Anthropic and warned that frontier AI labs were "gambling with our lives," Sanders seized on his comments. "Mr. Coxon is right," Sanders said on X, arguing that the people building advanced AI themselves have said it could pose catastrophic risks. After Amodei's blog post on Saturday, Sanders called on Trump to make the "deal of the century." "With the future of humanity at stake, Trump must negotiate a comprehensive treaty with President Xi of China to establish a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on super intelligence," he wrote on X. Francois Chollet, AI researcher Francois Chollet, an AI researcher who created Keras, an open-source software library, said on X that he hoped OpenAI and Anthropic were operating in good faith. "If these efforts are genuine, then oversight must take a more democratic and accountable form, with both national and international components," he said. He pointed to several signs he said would indicate that calls for more regulation are actually tricks for OpenAI and Anthropic to stifle competition. The warning signs he mentioned include calls to ban open-sourced AI and to hinder non-frontier research. Gavin Baker, venture capitalist Bloomberg/Getty Images Venture capitalist Gavin Baker said an executive order from President Donald Trump "seems likely after all this." "It is possible to democratize and distribute AI broadly and safely without centralizing it in the hands of a few corporations," he said on X. Baker said the most concrete development so far is the decision by OpenAI and Anthropic to bring in outside evaluators, a move he said could help the companies show they took reasonable steps to prevent harm. Still, he cautioned against regulations that would concentrate control of powerful AI systems among a handful of companies. "I do not want a few humans in control of intelligence," Baker wrote. Aaron Levie, CEO of Box Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch Aaron Levie, the cofounder and CEO of Box, a cloud content company, said Amodei's goals, as laid out in his essay, are "absolute necessities in AI development." "It completely stands to reason that we want these systems to be safe and 'aligned,'" Levie said on X. Levie said he didn't think Amodei is seeking undue regulation that would hobble Anthropic's open-source competitors. "How we get there — without meaningfully slowing down innovation progress or reducing competition — is one of the most complex questions in the 21st century, but the need is clearly real," he said. Chamath Palihapitiya, venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya. JC Olivera/Variety via Getty Images Venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya said Anthropic is now caught in a contradiction of its own making. If employees genuinely believe the company's technology could pose an existential threat, he said, that creates major liability and disclosure problems as Anthropic prepares for a possible IPO. "They do have to choose," Palihapitiya said on the "All-In" podcast. He said Anthropic must either distance itself from Coxon's warnings or accept their implications. He was also skeptical of the extinction scenarios themselves, saying the chain of events required for AI to wipe out humanity still seemed highly implausible. Gary Marcus, AI researcher and author Gary Marcus, the famed AI contrarian, said AI as it exists now poses little threat. "I am tired of the cosplay and am going to blunt," he wrote on X on Sunday. "The main kind of AI we need to worry about is general purpose AI agents that are hooked up to the internet. Most of them are unreliable, unable to systematically follow instructions. Coupled with internet access they can hack credentials and websites; given time they can probably do a lot worse," he wrote. He added that the problem isn't that AI agents are too smart, it's that they are too dumb, which he said is obvious by the way they can't follow instructions. "We don't (yet) need slowdowns. And we certainly don't need to panic ," he wrote. "We just need to take an unsafe product off the market." Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer Bloomberg/Getty Images Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, said on X that alignment could become the main constraint on how quickly companies can scale increasingly powerful AI systems. "Alignment is fundamental to delivering personal superintelligence for everyone," he said, using the techie term for AI following human instructions and not going rogue. Satya Nadella, chairman and CEO of Microsoft Satya Nadella said tktk Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO and chairman, said he welcomes Amodei's concept of embedded evaluators and "the broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this more than just talk." "The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia," he said on X. Nadella said that Microsoft will soon publish a "code of conduct" for Microsoft's AI models. "Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it's not worth pursuing," he said. items.summary_html:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei agreed this week to put third-party safety monitors in their companies.

Getty Images

  • AI leaders are rallying around calls to slow frontier AI development over mounting safety fears.
  • Dario Amodei warned that AI swarms could take over the internet within a year.
  • Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and Demis Hassabis backed Amodei's push for greater safeguards.

It took the possibility of species annihilation, but AI leaders did something remarkable this weekend: They reached a consensus.

After ex-Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon's warnings about a looming AI armageddon lit a firestorm among techies and politicians alike, the leaders of the most advanced AI labs came to a tentative agreement — largely via posts on X — that some sort of slowdown is necessary to save humanity.

While they were largely short on details regarding the mechanics of such a thing, and notable China has not weighed in, the American AI industry has reached an inflection point that could impact everything from your phone's chatbot to global politics.

"The stakes are too high for pacing to be an empty exercise — we need to use the time it gives us wisely," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in an essay entitled "We must pace the frontier," which was published Saturday.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who has made similar calls in the past, agreed in an X post later that day. So did Elon Musk. Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis also offered his support for Amodei's proposals.

Here's a look at what smart people are saying about the AI apocalypse and the methods the leaders of the leading AI labs say are necessary to stop it.

David Sacks, a presidential advisor on science and tech
David Sacks, former White House AI czar, expressed some skepticism over Anthropic's mythos warnings.

Matt McClain/The Washington Post/Getty Images

The Trump administration has repeatedly signaled disinterest in regulating AI development as it seeks to keep pace with China. David Sacks, a presidential advisor on science and tech and the former White House AI Czar, reiterated that stance on Saturday, with a bit of a twist.

"Dario has written that we need to 'pace the frontier,' and Sam has agreed. People may be surprised by my response: go ahead," Sacks wrote on X. "But stop pretending you need anyone else's permission."

Sacks browbeat OpenAI and Anthropic in his post, saying that the companies didn't want to slow down for altruistic reasons, but to gain favor in the markets.

"If you do, you'll buy goodwill for the next conversation," he said of a slowdown. "If you don't, we'll know this was just another bid for regulatory capture — or an election-season psyop."

Clément Delangue, Hugging Face CEO

Bloomberg/Getty Images

The CEO of Hugging Face, which was itself the victim of a notorious attack in July by OpenAI agents who schemed, communicated, and lied to evade detection, said AI safety can't be left solely to frontier labs.

Hugging Face, as an open-source-focused AI company, has long pushed for models and research to be shared more openly rather than kept behind closed doors.

Delangue said his company was launching what he called the "open alignment initiative," and asked that it be included in Amodei's proposed third-party evaluator program.

"Let's make AI safer by making it more transparent!" he wrote.

Jason Calacanis, investor
Jason Calacanis said that the ban was "smart" because of the risk of terrorism.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Investor, host of the "All-In" podcast, and industry expert Jason Calacanis is a lot more dubious than others that AI could actually cause the end of the world.

In an X post, Calacanis said Anthropic and OpenAI, whose most advanced models are not open-sourced, are attempting to kneecap open-source AI companies by pushing for regulations that would be far easier for deep-pocketed incumbents to comply with.

"If you want safety, you want disclosure — and open source is the ultimate disclosure process," he wrote.

In a follow-up post tagging Amodei, Calacanis said, "Don't go crying to the government and beg them to slow down open source models."

Bernie Sanders, Vermont senator
Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders.

Ken Cedeno / AFP via Getty Images

The senator from Vermont proposed legislation on September 3 that would ban the development and deployment of artificial superintelligence and temporarily pause the development of advanced AI systems.

After Coxon resigned from Anthropic and warned that frontier AI labs were "gambling with our lives," Sanders seized on his comments.

"Mr. Coxon is right," Sanders said on X, arguing that the people building advanced AI themselves have said it could pose catastrophic risks.

After Amodei's blog post on Saturday, Sanders called on Trump to make the "deal of the century."

"With the future of humanity at stake, Trump must negotiate a comprehensive treaty with President Xi of China to establish a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on super intelligence," he wrote on X.

Francois Chollet, AI researcher

Francois Chollet, an AI researcher who created Keras, an open-source software library, said on X that he hoped OpenAI and Anthropic were operating in good faith.

"If these efforts are genuine, then oversight must take a more democratic and accountable form, with both national and international components," he said.

He pointed to several signs he said would indicate that calls for more regulation are actually tricks for OpenAI and Anthropic to stifle competition.

The warning signs he mentioned include calls to ban open-sourced AI and to hinder non-frontier research.

Gavin Baker, venture capitalist

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Venture capitalist Gavin Baker said an executive order from President Donald Trump "seems likely after all this."

"It is possible to democratize and distribute AI broadly and safely without centralizing it in the hands of a few corporations," he said on X.

Baker said the most concrete development so far is the decision by OpenAI and Anthropic to bring in outside evaluators, a move he said could help the companies show they took reasonable steps to prevent harm.

Still, he cautioned against regulations that would concentrate control of powerful AI systems among a handful of companies. "I do not want a few humans in control of intelligence," Baker wrote.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box

Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch

Aaron Levie, the cofounder and CEO of Box, a cloud content company, said Amodei's goals, as laid out in his essay, are "absolute necessities in AI development."

"It completely stands to reason that we want these systems to be safe and 'aligned,'" Levie said on X.

Levie said he didn't think Amodei is seeking undue regulation that would hobble Anthropic's open-source competitors.

"How we get there — without meaningfully slowing down innovation progress or reducing competition — is one of the most complex questions in the 21st century, but the need is clearly real," he said.

Chamath Palihapitiya, venture capitalist
Chamath Palihapitiya.

JC Olivera/Variety via Getty Images

Venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya said Anthropic is now caught in a contradiction of its own making.

If employees genuinely believe the company's technology could pose an existential threat, he said, that creates major liability and disclosure problems as Anthropic prepares for a possible IPO.

"They do have to choose," Palihapitiya said on the "All-In" podcast. He said Anthropic must either distance itself from Coxon's warnings or accept their implications.

He was also skeptical of the extinction scenarios themselves, saying the chain of events required for AI to wipe out humanity still seemed highly implausible.

Gary Marcus, AI researcher and author

Gary Marcus, the famed AI contrarian, said AI as it exists now poses little threat.

"I am tired of the cosplay and am going to blunt," he wrote on X on Sunday.

"The main kind of AI we need to worry about is general purpose AI agents that are hooked up to the internet. Most of them are unreliable, unable to systematically follow instructions. Coupled with internet access they can hack credentials and websites; given time they can probably do a lot worse," he wrote.

He added that the problem isn't that AI agents are too smart, it's that they are too dumb, which he said is obvious by the way they can't follow instructions.

"We don't (yet) need slowdowns. And we certainly don't need to panic," he wrote. "We just need to take an unsafe product off the market."

Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, said on X that alignment could become the main constraint on how quickly companies can scale increasingly powerful AI systems.

"Alignment is fundamental to delivering personal superintelligence for everyone," he said, using the techie term for AI following human instructions and not going rogue.

Satya Nadella, chairman and CEO of Microsoft
Satya Nadella said tktk

Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images

Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO and chairman, said he welcomes Amodei's concept of embedded evaluators and "the broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this more than just talk."

"The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia," he said on X.

Nadella said that Microsoft will soon publish a "code of conduct" for Microsoft's AI models.

"Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it's not worth pursuing," he said.
