items.title: A Florida investor explains how he bought 3 condos for $360,000 and turned them into cash-flowing rentals using the 1% rule
items.summary: Florida-based couple Ted and Jamie Garber own more than 20 rental units in Florida. Ted Garber Florida-based investor Ted Garber walks Business Insider through one of his deals. He bought a 3-condo portfolio for $360,000 in 2022. He shares how he financed it and turned it into a cash-flowing asset. Ted Garber did not set out to become a long-distance landlord, but after struggling to find the cash flow he wanted close to home, he broadened his search. Looking at neighboring counties "really opened up the opportunities for us," the part-time investor, who has built a portfolio of Florida rentals alongside his wife, Jamie, told Business Insider. In September 2022, the Garbers bought three occupied condos listed together for $360,000. The properties were about a 90-minute drive from their Florida home. It was their first out-of-area acquisition — and an experiment to see whether they could self-manage rentals without being on-site regularly. Four years later, Garber said they have visited the properties just once and spend less than an hour a week managing their broader portfolio of 29 tenants. He opened the books on the deal and shared how he picked the condos, financed the purchase, and turned the portfolio into a cash-flowing asset. BI verified the purchase and the Garbers' ownership of the three condos by reviewing the final ALTA Settlement Statement and new landlord letters showing the rent for each unit. A portfolio that passed the 1% rule Garber found the three-condo portfolio on LoopNet, where the listed gross rent immediately caught his attention. At the $360,000 purchase price, the condos generated $3,675 in combined monthly rent, just over 1% of the price. That satisfied Garber's initial screening tool: the 1% rule . The rule of thumb suggests that a property's monthly rent should be at least 1% of its purchase price to have a reasonable chance of generating positive cash flow. It is not a guarantee, but it is a quick way to decide whether a listing is worth investigating further. He also saw room to increase rents, which he determined were below market, and liked the stable area outside Orlando's Disney corridor. To make the numbers work, however, he had to negotiate. The condo portfolio was initially listed for between $390,000 and $400,000, he said. That's a typical step in his process, he added: "I always negotiate. If it's really a steal, I'll do full asking immediately with a seller concession or something." Due diligence and the purchase Before making an offer, Garber makes sure his financing is in place. In this case, the couple financed the purchase with a commercial loan amortized over 20 years at an interest rate of roughly 5.5%. He said they put 25% down and invested $113,548 in total, including the down payment and transaction costs. Because the condos were occupied, Garber reviewed the existing leases, comparable rents, HOA finances and reserves, association rules, and the condition of each unit. His wife attended the inspection, giving the couple an opportunity to see all three homes while tenants were in place. Deal Detail Figure Purchase date September 2022 Property type Three occupied condos Purchase price $360,000 Total cash invested $113,548 Down payment 25% Financing Commercial loan, 20-year amortization, ~5.5% rate Initial combined monthly rent $3,675 Combined monthly rent as of 2026 $4,530 Current monthly loan payment $1,744.83 Principal repaid $30,041 over about four years Rent rose, but so did costs The portfolio's combined monthly rent has risen from $3,675 at acquisition to $4,530 today. Its monthly expenses include: Loan payment: $1,744.83 Property taxes: $500 Insurance: $408.78 HOA fees: $906.01 Garber said HOA dues and insurance costs have roughly doubled since purchase, reflecting rising insurance rates and inflation. Those expenses have reduced the portfolio's returns, though he still considers the deal "very healthy." The 20-year loan has also helped build equity relatively quickly: $721.05 of the current monthly payment goes toward principal. Garber said the portfolio's tenants have paid down $30,041 of the debt, or about 12%, over roughly four years. "We're getting monthly cash flow, and our tenants are paying off the mortgage," he said. The rent strategy: below-market rates Garber could likely charge more for the condos. Instead, he prefers to keep rents at or slightly below market. The strategy is partly financial — lower rents can mean fewer vacancies, lower turnover costs, and less time spent finding new tenants — but it also reflects the kind of landlord Garber wants to be. "When you do rent to people that are below market or at market, they're really thankful for that," he said. "They take care of your properties for you a little bit better." Garber is still looking for deals, but he said higher interest rates and strong property values in his market make it harder to find leveraged investments that produce more than 8% to 10% cash-on-cash returns. He would still seek properties that combine monthly cash flow with built-in equity — especially listings that may be overlooked because of weak marketing, poor photos, or other correctable issues. "You make money on the buy," he said. Asked what he would do differently with the three-condo portfolio, Garber's answer was simple: "We would have bought more." items.title: Why AI researchers keep building something they think will kill humans
items.summary: A masked protester holds a placard saying 'Skynet Just Woke Up' in reference to the Terminator movies in London during a 2021 anti-lockdown demonstration. ZUMA Press Wire via Reuters Connect A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for the weekly AI Insider newsletter here . On Tuesday, OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar headlined a packed Goldman Sachs tech conference in San Francisco. One thing she said really stood out to me: The company's biggest models can now train other smaller models, helping OpenAI save on the huge costs of training these systems. This is an example of recursive self improvement, or RSI, where AI gets so powerful it can create the next, even more powerful, system itself. For the Wall Street analysts and investors around me at the Goldman conference, this sounded like an amazing business opportunity. For Silicon Valley, especially some hardcore AI researchers, it's terrifying. Now that summer is over, there's a realization that RSI is either here already or coming very soon. There's a chance AI systems will get way more powerful very quickly. Add in the rise of AI agents swarming across the internet doing both great and worrying things, like breaking out of their "sandbox" testing environments, and you have full-blown panic in some parts of the AI community. "We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic , wrote on X this week. Other employees from Anthropic and OpenAI weighed in too, setting off a firestorm across the valley. "Nonsense" Back at the Goldman conference on Thursday, I ran into Brad Gerstner from Altimeter Capital, an investor in Anthropic and OpenAI. Will AI kill humans I asked? "It's fucking nonsense," he said. For the Wall Street crowd, it's head-scratching why, right before what could be the biggest IPO in history, Anthropic employees would say their main product will kill humans. So why would these people keep working on AI development when they think it will kill people? Here are some theories, some gathered this week and others from discussing and thinking about this for longer. "Commercial incentives" First up, the money reason. Anthropic and OpenAI will succeed by creating better AI and selling it. So they must keep going, and employees are along for the ride, even if they feel awful about the technology being potentially dangerous. Second, some researchers, especially at Anthropic, feel they are the only ones who can be trusted to keep this technology safe, so they must keep pushing ahead of everyone else. If Anthropic pauses and OpenAI or Chinese labs move ahead, that would be even worse because those other groups cannot be trusted with powerful AI. Samuel Marks, scalable oversight lead at Anthropic, put these reasons in writing this week, a stunningly admission. "Why do AI developers continue despite the risk? Due to a mixture of commercial incentives and a belief that they are in a race with other, less responsible AI developers that will abuse the technology or develop it less safely," he wrote on X. Recruiting reason Another explanation comes down to recruiting. AI researchers usually come from academia, not the business world, so they are very focused on doing good. This means a company like Anthropic can't say, "Come work here, and we'll create the most powerful profit-generating machine in history, and you'll become wildly rich." Instead, you pitch them on how this technology is so dangerous that they have to come work on AI safety and alignment to "save the world." This is much easier for researchers to swallow and makes them feel less guilty about getting rich from developing AI. It also makes them more likely to issue doom-laden predictions about an apocalyptic future. Loss of agency Then there's this explanation from Kylan Gibbs , CEO of AI startup Inworld, who thinks deeply about this stuff. This week's extreme AI doomerism is driven by a growing loss of agency, he told me. As AI becomes dramatically more powerful, control over its development is becoming concentrated in the hands of a few labs. Even researchers inside those companies can feel they have little influence over AI's direction, leaving them with high awareness of the risks but little control over the outcome. That gap between awareness and agency fuels anxiety — and that spills out in the form of public warnings about existential risk. This is not lost on AI leaders. "People really need agency," Sam Altman said on a podcast earlier this year. "People want agency, self-determination, the ability to play a role in architecting the future alongside the rest of society." I think we all feel this right now as AI spreads so quickly through our lives and work. Sign up for BI's AI Insider newsletter here . Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Attention shoppers: digital ad screens are about to be everywhere you look
items.summary: Amazon has specific rules about what types of ads can be shown on the screens at Whole Foods. Dominick Reuter/Business Insider Retailers have gradually added digital display ads to their stores for the past year. Now the pace is picking up as the concept gains wider acceptance with Walmart and Walgreens. A survey this year found that shoppers' acceptance of ad screens depends on the in-store context. Trips to the store used to offer a break from the digital screens that dominate modern life. Those days are winding down . Retailers are now trying to bring more advertising into stores by selling brands access to screens in aisles, endcaps, and checkouts, where customers make their final decisions . Walmart, Walgreens, Amazon, and grocery chains are betting that the screens can help shoppers find relevant products while opening a new source of high-margin revenue. "We do see a meaningful opportunity there to have more engaging screens throughout the store," Walmart's head of advertising, Ryan Mayward, said this week at a conference hosted by Goldman Sachs. Walmart has a large and growing online ad business , and it already has a lot of screens in its stores, mostly located in perimeter areas like the deli, bakery, or electronics sections. The next step is to bring some of that online ad information to an in-store shopping experience. Now, Mayward said the retail giant is testing options in higher-traffic areas, like aisle endcaps. These displays would include up-to-date information about inventory and pricing that could entice shoppers to venture down an aisle for a sponsored product. "We're really excited about using the store and introducing new advertising services," Mayward added. Although Walmart is the largest retailer to adopt the tech, it's far from the first. Walgreens is partnering with Looma to add digital displays to 1,200 stores. The drugstore chain said it is partnering with in-store advertising firm Looma to outfit about 1,200 locations with screens, starting in October, to serve ads near specific merchandise. Brands under the Albertson's banner have also seen more screens pop up in their stores after the company launched a test last year of jumbo displays at the entrance and in the produce section. And while the initial use case for in-store digital ads is to highlight merchandise in-store, retailers are already looking at ways to sell ads for other products and services as well. Mayward said these "non-endemic" ad placements are starting to appear on its recently acquired Vizio TV platform and in the Walmart app, from businesses such as fast-food restaurants, insurance agencies, and local car dealerships. items.title: I visited Capital One's lounge at LaGuardia. I loved the free steak and shrimp, but I'll do 1 thing differently next time.
items.summary: The author got to LaGuardia Airport over three hours early to fully experience the Capital One Landing. Jane Zhang Business Insider editor Jane Zhang utilized Capital One's lounge at LaGuardia Airport ahead of her flight home. Thanks to lounge access through her credit card, she enjoyed tapas, steak, shrimp, and mocktails. She enjoyed her experience, but would've preferred self-service options and being seated in a different section. Anyone who knows me knows that I'm not a timely person. Even in higher-stakes situations like flights, my time blindness is hard to overcome. (I've definitely gotten to the airport 45 minutes before takeoff on at least one occasion before.) So when I showed up at LaGuardia Airport last week, three and a half hours early for my flight home to Chicago, it was a first-time experience for me. However, it wasn't entirely out of character — because another thing about me is that I love a good deal . In this case, the good deal was getting my money's worth at the new Capital One Landing that opened in February. Here's how I got access to it, and how I made the most of the experience. My credit card gives me lounge access The Capital One Venture X is my first-ever credit card that includes airport lounge access . With its $395 annual fee, it gives me access to Capital One's seven airport lounges (two of which are designed as sit-down restaurant-style culinary concepts, which Capital One calls "Landings," including the one I visited) as well as Priority Pass lounges worldwide. Unfortunately for me, there is no Capital One lounge in Chicago, where I live, so I was elated when I saw that the Capital One Landing at LaGuardia had opened ahead of my trip to New York. Previously, Venture X holders used to be able to bring up to two guests into Capital One lounges for free, and authorized users on Venture X cards also could get complimentary entry to the lounges. That changed in February 2026. Now, authorized users like my husband must pay a $125 fee annually to get complimentary access to the lounges, or I could pay a guest fee of $45 for him each time. Before leaving for our New York trip, my husband and I discussed and decided that it felt worth it to pay the $125 annual fee for him. After all, we reasoned, we're bound to spend at least $20 a person on food at the airport anyway, so this will pay itself off after three round-trip flights. And since we have several trips planned for the next year, it's more cost-effective than paying for a guest pass for him each time. I showed up earlier than I probably ever have in my life We're allowed to enter the lounge up to three hours prior to takeoff, and I wanted to make sure we got there as early as possible. Maximizing time was especially important since we were flying out of a different terminal (Terminal C) than the one the lounge was in (Terminal B). There's no way to transit between terminals after security, so we had to make sure to give ourselves enough time to exit the terminal, take the shuttle bus over to Terminal C, and go through security again. My flight was at 6:45 p.m., so my goal was to be at the airport by a little after 3 p.m., to give us time to get through security and to the Landing before 3:45 p.m. Through the Capital One app, I was also able to make a reservation for 3:45 p.m., out of an abundance of caution, in case the lounge was extremely busy and filled up that day. We got in an Uber at 2:40 p.m., got to the airport by 3 p.m., and were through security by 3:12 p.m. It was particularly quick because it was a quiet afternoon, and we both have TSA PreCheck access through Global Entry (another benefit of the Venture X card) . By 3:15 p.m., we were already at the Capital One Landing, located just beyond the food court after security. The Capital One Landing opened in LaGuardia Airport's Terminal B in February 2026. Jane Zhang Since we were already there, we decided to try our luck and ask if it was possible to enter sooner (again, as a chronically late person, a rare occurrence for me). Unfortunately, the check-in machine wouldn't allow for it, so we left and found some seats in the food court in front of a giant TV showing the US Open, where my husband asked me, almost out of instinct, "Want a snack?" "No," I reminded him. "The lounge has snacks!" We had to save ourselves for the free food — or I should say, "free" food — that our annual fees had afforded us. The food was tasty Earlier that day, I'd sought input from my colleague and aviation expert Taylor Rains , who recommended arriving hungry, trying out the various ways to order food, and remembering to tip the bar staff if we order drinks. Once we checked in at the lounge — which wasn't very busy after all — we were brought to a table, where the staff member reminded us that everything there was complimentary and explained the two ways we could order food: We could get tapas-style cold plates from the bar or order hot food using the QR code on the table. For beverages, there were also a variety of alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks that could be ordered for table service, as well as a coffee bar. There was a variety of tapas-style cold dishes at the bar, as well as bartenders preparing cocktails and drinks. Jane Zhang My husband and I each took multiple trips up to the bar for food, as well as put in several rounds of table service hot dishes. From the bar, my favorites were the cured meats, vinegar-cured anchovies, and mango and coconut sticky rice. I found the salt-cured anchovies too salty for my taste. Tapas options included cured meats, anchovies, hummus, Caesar salad, gazpacho, htipiti, and cheese. Jane Zhang For dessert, there was flan, cheesecake, mango and coconut sticky rice, and strawberries with cream. Jane Zhang The real treat, though, was the table service hot food. Out of the various small dishes we tried, my husband and I thoroughly enjoyed the steak with mojo verde sauce and shrimp — and not just because we couldn't believe we could get steak and shrimp for free — as well as a guava mocktail called the "Flamingo Shuttle." One of several rounds of food we ordered and got from the bar. Jane Zhang The space was nice and felt like a café or restaurant The vibe of the Landing overall felt almost like a restaurant. We were brought to a table rather than just walking in and choosing one to put our stuff down at, as is the case with most of the other airport lounges we've been to. The table we were seated at was relatively close to the bar and was in front of giant floor-to-ceiling windows that overlooked the planes on the tarmac. The lounge had floor-to-ceiling windows, allowing for excellent natural lighting and a great view of the tarmac while we ate. Jane Zhang There was also a rather restaurant-esque style of service embedded in the experience. When getting food from the bar, instead of being a buffet-style where we'd help ourselves, all of the food was tucked away behind glass display cases, and members of staff would put the food onto plates and hand them to us. My husband and I both agreed we would've preferred a self-serve format for the bar area, both so we wouldn't need to inconvenience a staff member with needing to select the food for us, and also so we'd have more agency in getting the portions we wanted for ourselves, instead of needing to awkwardly ask for more. The bathrooms of the lounge were all-gender, single-stall bathrooms. There were five of them, and the one I used was clean, spacious, and simple, with a box of tissues and a bottle of lotion available. The bathroom was clean and spacious. Jane Zhang There's one thing I'd do differently next time After nearly an hour of enjoying the food and surroundings of the Landing, I thought I had a good sense of everything it had to offer. However, after exiting the bathroom, I realized there was an entire other dining room that I hadn't seen, tucked away past the bathrooms. In addition to a wall of floor-to-ceiling windows, a large portion of the ceiling itself was also made of glass, which made for a beautiful greenhouse vibe. I slightly regretted not sitting in this other, better-lit dining area. Jane Zhang Knowing what I know now, the next time we fly through LaGuardia and come to the Capital One Landing, I'll be sure to ask to be seated in that area, if possible. We left feeling very full, happy, and relaxed Having access to this airport lounge ended up serving multiple purposes for my husband and me: It pushed me to avoid my chronically late tendencies and actually get to the airport extremely early, saved us from spending $40 on mediocre airport fast food, and allowed us to indulge our love for buffets by trying the various dishes and drinks available without an additional cost. After about two hours, we left extremely content and in a great mood, ready to head over to Terminal C, go through security again, and take a nap on our two-hour flight back to Chicago. And remembering the advice from my colleague Taylor, we made sure to leave a tip with the bartenders on the way out. Do you have a story to share about airport lounges? Contact this reporter at janezhang@businessinsider.com . Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: A laid-off Grubhub worker created a tracker to help others find jobs. 18 months later, recruiters are learning from it.
items.summary: Irvin Thevaranjan has managed a tracker for laid-off Grubhub workers over the past year and a half. Irvin Thevaranjan Tech and related industries continue to get hit with layoffs. One laid-off Grubhub employee built a community to help coworkers navigate the aftermath. It's helped laid-off workers find jobs and recover from losing their roles. Irvin Thevaranjan was blindsided by his layoff. The day before, the head of governance risk and controls at delivery service Grubhub had a stellar performance review with his boss, who told him that he had lots of opportunities in front of him at the company. Less than a day later, though, he found himself on a call where most participants weren't visible, and no one could unmute themselves. "That's when I was like 'Oh crap, this is the wrong call to be on,'" he said. In the hours afterward, Thevaranjan started piecing together a list of the hundreds of others who lost their jobs at Grubhub that day in February 2025. Then, he had an idea: What if he created a list of everyone who was laid off that day to help them find new opportunities? One-and-a-half years later, Thevaranjan still runs the Ex-Grubhub Talent Network, which has listed 326 laid-off alumni looking for work after layoffs. Most have found new jobs, according to the tracker. "Irvin makes it his personal mission to get everybody employed," said Paul de Lucena, a former Grubhub employee and network member. Workers at tech companies from Amazon to Meta to Uber have faced layoffs this year . Many have to figure out what's next with their own networks — or, perhaps, with some help from a group chat of fellow laid-off employees that goes dark after a month or two. Thevaranjan's network represents something different, according to former Grubhub employees and others who have interacted with it: A grassroots effort to provide the support that's typically lacking after a layoff. From the 'empathy window' to a tracker The most publicly visible part of the network is a tracker that Thevaranjan built to showcase laid-off employees and their experience to potential employers. There's also a Slack workspace where laid-off workers commiserate over the job search, share links to open roles, and post about their hobbies. Grubhub workers who were more recently laid off can also join the group by filling out a Google Form that Thevaranjan and other administrators review. Thevaranjan said he got the idea from Kristen Ubaldi, the former chief people officer at Groupon. Ubaldi created a similar list and promoted it with the help of Groupon's executives after the company laid off employees in 2020. Originally, the Ex-Grubhub Network was mostly about helping folks navigate the days after the layoff, Thevaranjan told Business Insider. He recalled introducing a laid-off colleague to a recruiter at Reddit, where Thevaranjan had previously interviewed, the same day as they were laid off. "It's not even about getting him a job," Thevaranjan said. "It's the fact that he feels supported." Thevaranjan said he drew on his skills as an auditor to create the list of laid-off employees. To get more eyes on it, though, he tagged some of Grubhub's executives in a LinkedIn post days after the layoffs. "I call it the empathy window, this short period of time where people feel bad for you," he said. As Thevaranjan kept promoting his effort on LinkedIn, the network attracted more laid-off Grubhub employees — as well as others interested in what he was doing. Katie Cavote, a former recruiter at Grubhub, said she advised Thevaranjan on how to make the network more attractive for recruiters at other companies to use. The two never knew each other when they were still at Grubhub. People who oversee hiring are often looking for candidates from a specific company or with a specific background, Cavote said. The tracker sorts laid-off workers by specialty to make that easier. "Recruiters are getting creative these days in finding the right talent," she said. C.J. Cross, who worked in workforce analytics at Grubhub, lost his job in the same 2025 layoffs as Thevaranjan. That summer, he started a new job at Uber thanks to a referral he got from the Ex-Grubhub Network. When he got laid off again earlier this month as part of Uber's cuts , he rejoined the community. "The very first thing I did was go back to the Grubhub group chat," he said. Anne Stamer, a career transition coach who led webinars for the ex-Grubhub Network, said that big career networking sites like LinkedIn provide lots of potential connections for recently laid-off workers. With millions of members, though, it can also be overwhelming to devise a strategy that leads to a new job. "It's a double-edged sword," she said. Tamara Pohle, another career-transition consultant who led webinars for the group with Stamer, said she hasn't seen another layoff support group last as long as the network that Thevaranjan created. A stream of tech layoffs over the last few years shows how weakened the connections between companies and their employees have become, Pohle said. The layoffs have also made the connections that Thevaranjan's group provides even more important. "Genuine human connection has never gone stale," she said. Ubaldi, the former Groupon chief people officer who created a similar list of laid-off employees, told Business Insider that she wanted to make it clear that the layoffs weren't the workers' fault. More companies should use their networks to help the people they're laying off, she said. "I don't know why more don't," she said. Have a tip? Contact this reporter at abitter@businessinsider.com or via encrypted messaging app Signal at 808-854-4501. Use a personal email address, a nonwork WiFi network, and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely. Read the original article on Business Insider

  • One laid-off Grubhub employee built a community to help coworkers navigate the aftermath.
  • It's helped laid-off workers find jobs and recover from losing their roles.

Irvin Thevaranjan was blindsided by his layoff.

The day before, the head of governance risk and controls at delivery service Grubhub had a stellar performance review with his boss, who told him that he had lots of opportunities in front of him at the company.

Less than a day later, though, he found himself on a call where most participants weren't visible, and no one could unmute themselves. "That's when I was like 'Oh crap, this is the wrong call to be on,'" he said.

In the hours afterward, Thevaranjan started piecing together a list of the hundreds of others who lost their jobs at Grubhub that day in February 2025. Then, he had an idea: What if he created a list of everyone who was laid off that day to help them find new opportunities?

One-and-a-half years later, Thevaranjan still runs the Ex-Grubhub Talent Network, which has listed 326 laid-off alumni looking for work after layoffs. Most have found new jobs, according to the tracker.

"Irvin makes it his personal mission to get everybody employed," said Paul de Lucena, a former Grubhub employee and network member.

Workers at tech companies from Amazon to Meta to Uber have faced layoffs this year. Many have to figure out what's next with their own networks — or, perhaps, with some help from a group chat of fellow laid-off employees that goes dark after a month or two.

Thevaranjan's network represents something different, according to former Grubhub employees and others who have interacted with it: A grassroots effort to provide the support that's typically lacking after a layoff.

From the 'empathy window' to a tracker

The most publicly visible part of the network is a tracker that Thevaranjan built to showcase laid-off employees and their experience to potential employers.

There's also a Slack workspace where laid-off workers commiserate over the job search, share links to open roles, and post about their hobbies. Grubhub workers who were more recently laid off can also join the group by filling out a Google Form that Thevaranjan and other administrators review.

Thevaranjan said he got the idea from Kristen Ubaldi, the former chief people officer at Groupon. Ubaldi created a similar list and promoted it with the help of Groupon's executives after the company laid off employees in 2020.

Originally, the Ex-Grubhub Network was mostly about helping folks navigate the days after the layoff, Thevaranjan told Business Insider. He recalled introducing a laid-off colleague to a recruiter at Reddit, where Thevaranjan had previously interviewed, the same day as they were laid off.

"It's not even about getting him a job," Thevaranjan said. "It's the fact that he feels supported."

Thevaranjan said he drew on his skills as an auditor to create the list of laid-off employees. To get more eyes on it, though, he tagged some of Grubhub's executives in a LinkedIn post days after the layoffs.

"I call it the empathy window, this short period of time where people feel bad for you," he said.

As Thevaranjan kept promoting his effort on LinkedIn, the network attracted more laid-off Grubhub employees — as well as others interested in what he was doing.

Katie Cavote, a former recruiter at Grubhub, said she advised Thevaranjan on how to make the network more attractive for recruiters at other companies to use. The two never knew each other when they were still at Grubhub.

People who oversee hiring are often looking for candidates from a specific company or with a specific background, Cavote said. The tracker sorts laid-off workers by specialty to make that easier.

"Recruiters are getting creative these days in finding the right talent," she said.

C.J. Cross, who worked in workforce analytics at Grubhub, lost his job in the same 2025 layoffs as Thevaranjan. That summer, he started a new job at Uber thanks to a referral he got from the Ex-Grubhub Network.

When he got laid off again earlier this month as part of Uber's cuts, he rejoined the community. "The very first thing I did was go back to the Grubhub group chat," he said.

Anne Stamer, a career transition coach who led webinars for the ex-Grubhub Network, said that big career networking sites like LinkedIn provide lots of potential connections for recently laid-off workers.

With millions of members, though, it can also be overwhelming to devise a strategy that leads to a new job. "It's a double-edged sword," she said.

Tamara Pohle, another career-transition consultant who led webinars for the group with Stamer, said she hasn't seen another layoff support group last as long as the network that Thevaranjan created.

A stream of tech layoffs over the last few years shows how weakened the connections between companies and their employees have become, Pohle said. The layoffs have also made the connections that Thevaranjan's group provides even more important.

"Genuine human connection has never gone stale," she said.

Ubaldi, the former Groupon chief people officer who created a similar list of laid-off employees, told Business Insider that she wanted to make it clear that the layoffs weren't the workers' fault.

More companies should use their networks to help the people they're laying off, she said.

"I don't know why more don't," she said.

items.title: I own a house rental business near a future Meta AI data center. Construction workers make up most of our tenants.
items.summary: Angel and Bryan Crawford opened a mobile home park in northeast Louisiana in 2025. Angel Crawford Meta is building its largest data center to date in Richland Parish, Louisiana. Angel Crawford and her husband own 18 rental properties in the area. Crawford said RV and mobile home parks are booming due to the influx of workers. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Angel Crawford, who owns 18 rental properties in northeastern Louisiana and runs a third-party website connecting tenants with property owners. Construction for Meta's largest-ever AI data center has begun in Holly Ridge, an unincorporated community about 10 minutes away from her home in Delhi. My husband and I have been in Delhi for four years. We're originally from this area, but we've moved around because of our nursing careers. I was a quality manager, and my husband was a director of case management. We were empty nesters looking for something to do, so we started with real estate and rentals because they are very much needed in this area. It's very rural here, so when there are fluctuating prices in the market, it doesn't really hit us because there are never enough houses for sale or rent. In 2024, we started buying older houses that had been on the market for a long time or needed a lot of work. We had a vision to create a mobile home park and already purchased some land when we heard about Meta's data center. That's what pushed us to keep going forward. We understood there wasn't enough housing for residents, and our dream of building more multifamily houses was right in line to do that. Around here, people feel one way or the other about the data center. Either people are excited about the opportunities, or they hate it. There's no in between. I see it as an opportunity for us to have more experiences in our area and jobs for our children, so they can stay here instead of moving away. We began Parish Line Properties, which now operates 18 properties, in 2024. I also created StayNELA, a third-party website to connect listing agents with tenants, in 2025. The impact of Meta's data center on real estate Parish Line Properties has 18 homes, and 14 of those are workforce housing. Location is very important to Meta's workers because they work six to seven days a week and 12-plus hours a day. They leave around 4:30 in the morning, and they don't come home until 7 at night. One of the big things my tenants tell me is that if they live in Dallas and it's 30 miles to work, it takes about 30 minutes. Well, in rural areas, 30 miles could take 60 minutes because of all the back roads and little towns you have to go through. The closer they can get to the job site, the better. A fully-furnished four-bedroom, two-bathroom home that's eight miles from the data center costs an average of $3,000 a month. I don't have any problem with getting tenants in those homes at that price point. Before Meta arrived, an unfurnished house in the same area would probably go for around $1,200 to $1,500 a month. We've assured our local long-term tenants that we won't increase their rent. That's not what we're about. We're not going to put local tenants in a bind. We're going to find different and new properties to help with workforce housing. We opened our Antley Pines mobile home park in December 2025. We added two homes last December, four this May, and our last four in July. All the homes were secured by deposits from Meta workers before we even got them into the park. Separately, I created StayNELA because there weren't many resources for anybody who wasn't a local to find rental homes. I did a lot of research for several months by driving around the area and looking at all the different signs in people's yards or at four-way stops that you couldn't read properly. I kept a log, took pictures, and kept them in a folder on my phone. If anything was on Facebook about a rental, I saved it. When I finally took the leap to design a webpage, I reached out to everybody that I had found through phone numbers, Facebook posts, and listings. I'm not a real estate agent, so I'm helping people advertise. When I list a property, I include the owner's phone number so potential tenants can go straight to the owner of that house. My goal was to bridge that gap for people looking for rentals here from other states. The impact of Meta's data center on the local economy Each home in our mobile park is on one-fourth of an acre. After Meta's gone, we can sell them individually or rent them out. We've seen a lot of laundromats, RV parks, and mobile home parks come to the area. It's great for the economy in our area because people who we've worked with who install electrical systems, septic systems, plumbing, gravel, and all those things are busy because Meta's here. For example, getting a property surveyed is extremely hard, whereas it used to be pretty easy. Before, you could call them, and they'd say, "Yeah, I'll be there to come do your survey in a week or so." Now, you have to get on a list and wait for your turn. items.title: What happens when you tell Jensen Huang you're quitting Nvidia
items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Chris Jung/NurPhoto via Getty Images CEO Jensen Huang doesn't sugarcoat advice to Nvidia employees who quit. He critiqued one startup's name and told another founder his biggest weakness could hold him back. Founders said the tough love stuck — and they acted on his advice. As they were preparing to leave Nvidia, David Hoeller and Nikita Rudin anxiously hopped on a late-night call with their CEO. The two had spent years working on robotics at the chip giant, pushing the boundaries of simulation and helping pull off a demo in which CEO Jensen Huang took the stage with a coterie of humanoids. The pair wanted more freedom to bring that technology into the real world and left in 2024 to found Flexion Robotics, a startup building robot intelligence . As they dialed in from a conference in Munich, Huang didn't try to talk them out of leaving, though he did have one problem with their startup: its intended name, Checkpoint. "He told us that the name was bad, and that we had to change it," Rudin said, adding that they'd heard from others that the name sounded like it belonged in a different industry. "I don't want to give him all the credit, but we probably changed it because of his comment." Huang also warned them about the long road ahead. "His message was, 'We don't realize how tough a journey it's going to be,'" Rudin said. Flexion's experience offers a glimpse into how Huang counsels some departing founders: with encouragement and little sugarcoating. That directness extends through Nvidia's culture, where Huang is known for cutting through management layers and personally weighing in on everything from employee output to customer complaints . Flexion Robotics' David Hoeller and Nikita Rudin. Courtesy of Flexion Robotics Flexion's relationship with Nvidia didn't end there. Nvidia later invested in the Zurich-based company, which is now expanding into the US, having recently opened a San Francisco office and hired researchers from companies like Meta. In total, it has raised more than $57 million. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. Founders say Jensen Huang gives 'honest feedback' For Bing Xu, Huang's parting advice was more personal. Xu joined Nvidia after it acquired his first startup in 2024. He left earlier this year — walking away from a potentially life-changing sum of Nvidia equity , he said — to build another startup called INT21, which uses AI to improve chip software. After Xu shared his plans, Huang spent two hours with him and other Nvidia executives discussing his work and trying to convince him to stay. INT21 founder and CEO Bing Xu. INT21 Huang also offered a pointed critique. He said communication was Xu's biggest weakness and that it could limit his achievements. Xu had a tendency to assume others shared his technical knowledge, making his explanations difficult to follow — and Huang suggested that staying at Nvidia would be a better path, he recalled. "This is the most honest feedback I had in the past 10 years about myself," said Xu, who now works with a public relations firm. "I didn't think my communication would be such a big problem, but when Jensen told me, I decided I could take this opportunity to become a better version of myself." The conversation wasn't all tough love. Xu said he was dealing with high blood pressure and other health issues at the time, and Huang encouraged him to take time off and rest. He viewed both the concern and criticism as evidence that Huang wanted him to succeed. Have a tip? Contact this reporter via email at gweiss@businessinsider.com or Signal at @geoffweiss.25. items.title: AWS Introduces Pizza Bot: An Open Source Inbox for Background AI Agents
items.summary: AWS introduced Pizza Bot , as a self-hosted application for AI tasks that continue while users work elsewhere. It organizes completed results and pending decisions into an email-style inbox. Earlier versions served more than 2,000 people inside Amazon, supporting meeting preparation, email drafting, Slack summaries, CRM logging, and research. The public application was rebuilt as an open source project. Deployable: Yes. Pizza Bot offers macOS, Windows, and Linux desktop builds, and browser and terminal clients connected to a local or standalone backend. Its code is licensed under Apache 2.0. An Inbox for Asynchronous Work Pizza Bot separates tasks into All , the thread history; Unread , completed work awaiting review; and Action , work paused for approval or an answer. Users can organize threads into folders and inspect delegated workers in the Activity panel. Tasks can start manually, through cron schedules, or through webhooks. The server owns scheduling. After downtime, missed cron intervals produce 1 catch-up run instead of replaying every missed interval. Trigger occurrences are recorded durably. How the Runtime Works The application uses DeepAgents and LangGraph for stateful execution. A Hono API server owns runtime execution and storage. Electron and browser clients share a React interface, while all clients communicate with the server over HTTP and server-sent events. LangGraph checkpoints retain thread state and approval pauses; separate SQLite stores hold cross-thread memory and application metadata. Reconnecting clients can replay buffered events. Closing a thread or disconnecting a client does not stop a running server. However, quitting the desktop app stops its embedded server and ends active runs. Checkpoints preserve the thread, but the step in flight can be lost. An always-on backend is required for work to continue after that desktop app exits. Skills, Tools, and Approval Controls Pizza Bot supports Amazon Bedrock, Anthropic, Google Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter, and Ollama . Configure a provider under Settings > Providers before running tasks. The agent has scratch-file operations and a sandboxed JavaScript interpreter without network or host-filesystem access. It can delegate through task when ready skill workers exist. The filesystem layer separately supports explicit folder grants and persistent memory. MCP servers expose external tools. Each SKILL.md defines a worker’s instructions and scoped tool access. A skill becomes callable only when its declared dependencies are available. Existing Claude Code-compatible .mcp.json configurations are supported, and plugins package skills with MCP servers. Skill authors configure interruptOn and allowedDecisions to require approval for specific tools. Depending on that policy, users can approve, edit proposed arguments, or reject an action. These controls must be configured for the relevant tools. Interactive Explainer Run the illustrative custom-skill workflow below. Compare an always-on backend with an embedded desktop server, close the client during execution, and approve, edit, or reject the proposed action. Animation timing is illustrative; no external actions occur. PIZZA BOT / BACKGROUND WORK Illustrative custom skill Backend location Always-on server Embedded in desktop Run example Close desktop Client: Open Server: Running Checkpoint: None Worker Approval Result Start a research brief, then close the desktop while it runs. All 0 Unread 0 Action 0 Prepare a research brief The custom skill gates its publish tool with interruptOn. publish_brief({title: "Research brief"}) Proposed title Approve Edit Reject Read result Desktop closed Open the desktop to review its inbox. Simulation only. No external calls. Approval specification &&&&&&& Key Takeaways An inbox for background agents: Pizza Bot organizes task history in All, completed work in Unread, and requests for approval or input in Action. Tasks support manual, cron, and webhook triggers. Persistent execution with DeepAgents and LangGraph: Checkpoints preserve thread state and approval pauses. Tasks continue after client disconnection while the backend remains running. Multiple model providers: Pizza Bot supports Amazon Bedrock, Anthropic, Google Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter, and local models through Ollama. Configured providers and tools can receive task data. Scoped skills and configurable approvals: MCP servers expose tools, while SKILL.md files define specialist workers. Tool-specific policies let users approve, edit, or reject proposed actions. Self-hosted and deployable: Apache 2.0 code, desktop builds, and standalone backend options are available. Each SQLite data directory supports 1 backend process. Check out the Technical details and GitHub Repo . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. Need to partner with us for promoting your GitHub Repo OR Hugging Face Page OR Product Release OR Webinar etc.? Skill authors configure interruptOn and allowedDecisions to require approval for specific tools. Depending on that policy, users can approve, edit proposed arguments, or reject an action. These controls must be configured for the relevant tools.

Interactive Explainer

Key Takeaways
  1. An inbox for background agents: Pizza Bot organizes task history in All, completed work in Unread, and requests for approval or input in Action. Tasks support manual, cron, and webhook triggers.
  2. Persistent execution with DeepAgents and LangGraph: Checkpoints preserve thread state and approval pauses. Tasks continue after client disconnection while the backend remains running.
  3. Multiple model providers: Pizza Bot supports Amazon Bedrock, Anthropic, Google Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter, and local models through Ollama. Configured providers and tools can receive task data.
  4. Scoped skills and configurable approvals: MCP servers expose tools, while SKILL.md files define specialist workers. Tool-specific policies let users approve, edit, or reject proposed actions.
  5. Self-hosted and deployable: Apache 2.0 code, desktop builds, and standalone backend options are available. Each SQLite data directory supports 1 backend process.

items.summary: Much of the world’s wastewater is still treated using a century-old, energy-intensive process of pumping oxygen through tanks of sewage. Thames Water, the UK’s largest water company, is now trialing an alternative developed at Newcastle University that uses microbes and electrodes to break down waste. It both uses less energy and gives off ammonia that can be recovered and sold as fertilizer.

items.title: The Algebra of Encrypted Audiences
items.summary: Replication is topology. Readability is cryptography. A photo album, three devices, and one wrong assumption Say you keep a family photo album synced across three machines: your phone, your laptop, and a small server at home that also backs up files for the rest of the household. All three machines end up holding the encrypted bytes of that album — the home server has to, or it couldn’t sync them. But only two people, you and your spouse, should ever be able to see the photos themselves. This is a mundane requirement. It’s also where most storage systems quietly conflate two different things: where data is stored and who can read it . If the album lives in a shared folder with permission bits, “where it’s stored” and “who can read it” are the same fact, enforced by the same mechanism, at the same layer. Move the folder to a new machine, and you’ve also moved — or lost — the access decision. Widen replication for durability, and you’ve widened, by construction, the set of processes that have to be trusted not to leak it. Engineers have spent decades building systems that separate these concerns better: row-level security in databases, IAM policies in cloud storage, capability tokens in distributed filesystems. All of them work by adding a checkpoint — a piece of logic that intercepts a read request and asks “is this caller allowed to see this?” before returning data. That checkpoint is the part worth examining closely, because it has a structural weakness that has nothing to do with how well it’s implemented. The checkpoint problem An access-control check is external to the data. The bytes sit in storage; a separate system — a permissions table, a policy engine, an IAM role — decides whether a given request may retrieve them. This works exactly as long as every path to those bytes goes through the checkpoint. In practice, it rarely does, forever. A misconfigured storage bucket, a replica spun up without the same policy attached, a backup pipeline that copies data but not its access rules, an administrator with raw filesystem access — each of these bypasses the checkpoint without touching the data at all. The data was never actually protected; only the front door to it was. There’s a second, quieter cost. Replication and access control now have to be kept consistent with each other, across machines, indefinitely. Every new replica needs the policy re-applied. Every policy change needs to propagate to every replica before the old one is considered revoked. This is a distributed consistency problem bolted onto a security requirement, and the two rarely fail gracefully together. The underlying issue is that readability and storage location are being treated as one variable when they are actually two. Two sets, not one .me's model for this — documented in the project as the "Algebra of Contexts" — starts by naming those two variables separately, along with a third: T , the topology set — which machines or processes physically hold a piece of ciphertext. A , the audience set — which principals can actually decrypt it. P , the capability set — what operations, beyond reading, are permitted. These three sets don’t all live at the same layer, and it’s worth being precise about which one the code discussed below actually implements. The kernel — the ME class itself — is where A is concrete: it declares secret scopes, derives per-path key material, encrypts and decrypts, and fails closed on tampering. T is not a data structure inside that kernel at all. The kernel produces snapshots and encrypted branches; a separate layer of the same system decides where those bytes physically end up — replicated to a backup, synced to a second device, served from a particular node. That's an architectural fact, not a detail being glossed over: the album's three-device topology is a real scenario, but it's assembled from the kernel's output plus infrastructure outside the kernel, not modeled as a single T set inside ME. P sits in between — there is real policy metadata attached to wrapped keys, and the DSL has operations that act like capabilities, but there isn't yet a uniform algebra of read/write/delegate/revoke applied consistently across every scope. Treat P, below, as the least finished of the three. What the kernel does implement precisely is the relationship between T and A as a statement , even where T itself lives elsewhere: replicating ciphertext does not, by itself, change who can derive the key for it. A backup server, a CDN edge cache, a second device — all of them can hold copies of the bytes without ever being able to open them. Encryption does not make data disappear from topology. It changes membership in readability. A holder of the ciphertext that doesn’t hold the right key material holds nothing but bytes it cannot open — not because a policy told it no, but because the decryption itself fails. That’s worth being precise about too: this isn’t the absence of a check. Decryption is a check — it’s just one that’s fused into the act of reading, rather than a separate policy consulted before the read happens. What disappears isn’t checking; it’s the external checkpoint that can drift out of sync with the data it’s supposed to govern. Binding audience to a path, not a table Here is where this stops being an abstract set-theory statement and becomes something concrete in .me's kernel: audience membership is declared as a structural property of a path, at write time, using a single operator: _. me.wallet["_"]("secret"); me.wallet.income(100); me("wallet")        // undefined me("wallet.income") // 100 — read inside a kernel/session holding "secret" The call me.wallet["_"]("secret") registers wallet as a secret scope — internally, this commits a "secret"-tagged operation, records a redacted memory entry, and invalidates the relevant key caches, rather than writing the key material into the public memory/index surface. Ordinary values written under wallet afterward are stored through the encrypted branch/value path, using key material derived from that scope secret. me("wallet") itself returns undefined — not because the value was deleted, but because the public index the kernel maintains for ordinary reads deliberately excludes the roots of secret scopes. The second line matters as much as its output. me("wallet.income") returns 100 only because this snippet runs inside the same kernel instance that declared the scope — it already holds "secret" and can derive the matching key, a behavior the kernel's own axiom tests assert directly. A different kernel instance, or the same code running without that input, would get undefined at wallet.income too, exactly as it does at wallet. _("secret") doesn't know who your spouse is, and it doesn't grant her membership by itself. It defines what a member of A must be able to produce. Getting a second principal into A is a separate, deliberate act, and it isn't automatic just because a scope exists: she needs the scope secret, or key material derived from it, transmitted to her through some channel. .me includes one concrete mechanism for that transmission, rather than leaving it as "figure it out": wrapping a secret to a specific recipient's public key, using ECDH-ES key exchange, HKDF-SHA-256 for key derivation, and AES-256-GCM for the actual encryption, tested against both correct and deliberately corrupted recipients. A scope secret wrapped this way can be handed to exactly one additional principal — your spouse's device, identified by its public key — without appearing in plaintext anywhere except her endpoint. This wrapping is a separate step from declaring the scope with _; nothing couples the two automatically. That's the difference between "audience" as a description and "audience" as something actually constructed: the algebra says A is whoever can derive the key; the wrapping mechanism is one deliberate way a second principal gets there without the secret passing through anywhere it could leak. Nesting and refinement Once a scope exists, narrower paths beneath it inherit its requirement rather than needing a separate one: me.wallet.hidden.notes("private note"); If wallet.hidden declares its own, tighter scope, wallet.hidden.notes derives its key material by chaining that scope's secret with its ancestor's — the derivation is built from the full lineage of path, scope, and any active noise boundary, not from the leaf's secret alone. The relationship wallet.hidden ⊆ wallet in the path structure produces a corresponding relationship in the audience: whoever can derive the key for wallet.hidden must also satisfy wallet's requirement, but not the reverse. Refining the path and refining the audience are the same operation, expressed once, rather than a path hierarchy and a separate permission hierarchy that have to be kept aligned by hand. Deliberately breaking that inheritance Sometimes two secrets under the same structural path should share nothing. .me provides a second operator, ~, for exactly this — it resets the derivation chain at a chosen boundary. me.wallet["_"]("alpha"); me.wallet.hidden.notes("alpha-note"); me.wallet["~"]("noise"); me.wallet["_"]("beta"); me.wallet.hidden.seed("beta-seed"); After the ~ call, the kernel locates this active noise boundary and restarts key derivation from it — everything written under wallet afterward derives its key material starting from the noise value instead of continuing the previous chain. wallet.hidden.notes, written before the reset, and wallet.hidden.seed, written after, end up with genuinely different effective secrets — verified directly by the kernel's test suite, which checks that the two computed secrets are unequal. Structurally, both paths sit under the same parent. Cryptographically, they belong to unrelated audiences. The path tree and the audience relationships it implies are related, but the second is not a rigid function of the first — ~ is the escape hatch for the cases where they need to diverge. The cost of doing this at the storage layer None of this is free, and it’s worth being direct about that, because it’s the part a system like this can’t hide behind good design. Reading or writing inside a secret scope means deriving key material and running actual encryption or decryption on every access, rather than a cheap lookup in a plain index. Benchmarks on the kernel show secret-scope reads running roughly one to two orders of magnitude slower than equivalent public reads at moderate scale — not a rounding error, a real and measurable tax. This is the honest price of making A a cryptographic property of the data instead of a policy decision made once and cached: there is no way to check “is this reachable” without the actual key derivation happening, because the check and the access are the same operation. The corollary is a genuine gain in failure mode. A tampered or corrupted secret blob doesn’t return wrong data — it fails to decrypt at all, and the kernel’s contract tests confirm this explicitly for several tamper scenarios: a flipped bit in a ciphertext, a wrong scope key, a wrong noise boundary. There is no “the check passed, and the data happened to be corrupted” state, because there is no check separate from decryption to pass. The predicates fall out for free Once audience and topology are separate, most of the vocabulary usually needed to describe access levels stops being a list of special cases and becomes a small number of statements about set size — with the caveat that only A is something the kernel enforces directly: A public space is one with no encryption at all — A is not a bounded set, because there’s nothing to bound. A private space has A = {self}. A shared space has |A| ≥ 2 — more than one principal, still explicitly bounded, and reached deliberately via key wrapping rather than by declaring a scope alone. A replicated space has |T| > 1 — a fact about the surrounding stack’s storage and sync layer, orthogonal to what A is. A shared, replicated, encrypted space — the family photo album, decryptable by two principals, physically present on three machines — is A = {your key, your spouse’s key} enforced by the kernel, sitting inside a T = {phone, laptop, home-server} arrangement decided above it. Nothing about T being larger than A needs a separate access mechanism; A stays exactly what it was declared to be, regardless of how the surrounding system decides to distribute the ciphertext. What this buys you, and what it costs The practical consequence of binding audience to the ciphertext rather than to an external checkpoint is that replication and access control become genuinely independent variables — one enforced cryptographically inside the kernel, the other handled by whatever infrastructure moves bytes around it. You can widen T — for durability, for latency, for caching — without an access-control migration, because nothing about growing T touches how A is derived. You can narrow A without moving any bytes. There’s no permissions table that can drift out of sync with the data it’s supposed to govern, because there is no second table — only key material, which either derives the right secret or doesn’t. What you give up is uniform, predictable cost: every read against a member of A does real cryptographic work, every time, rather than a table lookup gated by a cached decision. You also give up convenient administrative override — there is no “admin bypass” for a scope whose key material you don’t hold, which is the point, but it does mean operational tooling has to be designed around the fact that even the person running the system cannot casually read a scope they weren’t given the means to derive. Whether that trade is worth it depends entirely on what you’re building. For data whose replication needs and whose audience needs move independently — backups, multi-device sync, anything shared with a small group but stored somewhere larger than that group — treating audience as an algebraic property of the ciphertext, enforced at the kernel that produces it, removes an entire class of consistency problems by construction, even while the question of where the resulting bytes travel is answered by a different part of the system. For workloads where cheap, uniform access and centralized administrative visibility matter more than that guarantee, the cost of doing real cryptography on every scoped read is a cost you’d be paying for a property you may not need. For workloads where cheap, uniform access and centralized administrative visibility matter more than that guarantee, the cost of doing real cryptography on every scoped read is a cost you’d be paying for a property you may not need.

items.title: How to Reduce Claude Tokens (and Actually Get More Out of Claude Code)
items.summary: What happened when I hit my 5-hour limit, ran /usage out of curiosity, and started digging into how to cut my Claude token usage down So this happened while I was just using Claude Code like normal. Fixing some bugs, refactoring a service layer that had gotten messy, asking it to write a few tests. Regular day. Then mid-session I hit the wall, 5 hour limit, done, wait it out. I’d hit that limit before and just shrugged it off. But this time I got curious and typed /usage. Not ready for what I saw. A full breakdown just sitting there: input tokens, output tokens, cache reads, cache writes, an estimated dollar cost for the session. I just stared at it for a bit. Then went and checked another session. Then another. And that’s when I started actually looking into how to reduce Claude tokens instead of just eating the limit every 5 hours. Now it’s a full habit. I check /usage after basically every session because the numbers genuinely never add up the way you'd think they should, and I've picked up a bunch of stuff that actually moves the needle on token usage. Here’s what I’ve learned so far, if you’re using Claude Code , paying for Claude Pro or Max , or just trying to cut down your Claude token usage in general. First, understand why your tokens disappear so fast Before you can reduce something, you need to know what’s actually eating it. Claude Code gives you a usage indicator that climbs up to 100%. Easy to assume that’s just a token counter, burn through X, hit 100%, you’re done. But it’s more complicated than that. Anthropic’s own docs say usage depends on a bunch of stuff: how long the conversation is, files attached, which model you picked, active features, even the reasoning effort level. And Pro runs on two separate limits, a rolling 5-hour session limit and a weekly one, and they don’t reset the same way either. So already: 100% ≠ a fixed number of tokens. How you use it changes how fast it burns. I only really got this after comparing my own sessions side by side. Three sessions, all 100%, completely different token costs Here’s the part that actually got me. Three separate sessions, all reported as 100% of my session limit , but the estimated cost behind each one was nowhere close to the same. Session 1, Sonnet, light edits ~130 input tokens, 780 output tokens 7.1M cache reads, 212.1K cache writes Cost: $2.52 Session 2, Opus, medium use ~168 input tokens, 295 output tokens 7.6M cache reads, 285.1K cache writes Cost: $3.73 Session 3, Sonnet, heavy agentic stuff ~3.5K input tokens, 982.8K output tokens 654M cache reads, 13.7M cache writes Cost: $7.58 Same subscription. Same 100%. Cost ranging from $2.52 to $7.58. That’s more than 3x difference for the exact same reported limit. That’s the moment it clicked that most of my token usage was going to stuff I could actually control. What’s quietly burning through your tokens A few things I didn’t appreciate until I saw the numbers, and these are the actual levers if you’re trying to reduce Claude token usage: 1. Model choice Sonnet is basically the efficient default for regular coding work, Opus is meant for the harder stuff: big refactors, gnarly debugging, architecture decisions. Using a top-tier model to rename a variable is like calling in an architect to change a lightbulb. It’ll work. It just burns way more tokens than the task needed. Fix: default to Sonnet, only switch to Opus for genuinely hard problems. 2. Context you’re dragging around Your prompt could be five words, “fix this bug,” but the model isn’t just looking at those five words. It’s dragging along the whole conversation history, project instructions, files it already read, old diffs, tool output. A tiny prompt can sit on top of a mountain of context. Fix: start fresh conversations more often instead of letting one thread run forever. Point Claude at specific files or line ranges instead of letting it read whole directories. 3. Cache tokens piling up That 654 million cache-read number in Session 3 doesn’t mean it generated 654 million tokens of new text. It means a massive pile of context was being reused over and over. Input plus output alone just doesn’t tell the real story of what actually happened in that session. Fix: the longer a session runs, the more that cached context stacks up. Closing out sessions and starting clean ones for unrelated tasks helps a lot. 4. Letting Claude read more than it needs A lot of token waste comes from Claude reading entire files, or entire folders, when it only needed a specific function or section. Fix: be specific. “Look at the handleSubmit function in form.js" burns way fewer tokens than "look at the form file." 5. Repeated back-and-forth on the same thing If Claude gets something slightly wrong and you correct it five times in a row, each correction adds to the context pile for the rest of the session. Fix: if something’s clearly off, it’s often cheaper to start a new prompt with more detail than to keep patching the same thread. Wait, is Anthropic actually charging me per token then? No, and this part trips a lot of people up. Subscription billing and API and Console billing are two different systems. That dollar number you see in /usage is basically an estimate, roughly what that same work would've cost if you'd paid for it through the API. It's not some extra charge on top of your flat $20 (or $100/$200 if you're on Max). So the number isn’t a bill. It’s more like a lens, and once you understand it you can actually see where your token usage is going instead of just watching a percentage bar climb. The real goal isn’t “fewer tokens,” it’s fewer wasted tokens Once I started tracking this stuff, a better question showed up: What’s the cheapest way to reliably get this task done? If Claude finishes a feature for $2, fine. If it finishes the same feature for $0.80 at the same quality, that’s better. But if some cheaper model does it for $0.20 and leaves you with three bugs to fix by hand, you didn’t actually save anything, you just moved the cost somewhere less obvious. So reducing tokens isn’t just about using less. It’s about not spending tokens on stuff that didn’t need them in the first place. A quick checklist for cutting down Claude token usage Start a new session for unrelated tasks instead of reusing one giant thread Point Claude at specific files or functions instead of whole directories Default to Sonnet, save Opus for genuinely hard reasoning tasks Give clear, detailed prompts up front instead of correcting repeatedly Check /usage regularly so you actually know what's driving your usage instead of guessing Break big tasks into smaller, scoped requests instead of one massive open-ended ask So how much AI do you actually get for $20? Honestly, there’s no single answer, and that’s kind of the whole point. How much real work you get out of it depends on: model choice, context size, conversation length, tool usage, task difficulty, and how disciplined your workflow is Pro is $20/month right now in the US, with a 5-hour session limit and a separate weekly one, both of which shift depending on how you use it. If you’re maxing out constantly, Anthropic’s Max tiers ($100 to $200/month) give you a lot more headroom, but before jumping up a tier, it’s worth trying to actually reduce how many tokens you’re burning on the $20 tier first. final thought Next time your usage bar hits 100%, don’t just glance at it and move on. Run /usage. Actually look at the breakdown. Ask which model did the work, how much context it was dragging around, and whether the task even needed that much horsepower in the first place. Because the real question was never “how much did I use.” It’s “what did I actually get done with it, and how much of that usage was actually necessary.” if you’ve also stared at a /usage breakdown confused, lmk what patterns you've noticed in your own sessions, or what's helped you cut down your token usage.
